t: What regulators said. What marketing says.
x: Official warnings, the selling tricks that come up again and again, and claims that do not survive contact with the research. Tirzepatide recall from compounding pharmacy Apothecary Pharma (US), 24 Sep 2026 Apothecary Pharma LLC of Cary, North Carolina, a compounding pharmacy (not the maker of Mounjaro or Zepbound), voluntarily recalled its tirzepatide injection 18 mg/mL and an NAD+ injection across the US. The reason in the FDA enforcement report: lack of assurance of sterility. The FDA classified the recall as Class II, meaning the product may cause temporary or medically reversible health effects, with serious problems unlikely. Compounded drugs are not FDA-approved. Anyone who has this product should contact their doctor; the lot numbers are listed in the FDA report. FDA warning letters to peptide sellers The FDA sends warning letters when it decides a firm is selling unapproved drugs. In several cases the agency stated plainly that a “for research purposes only” label changes nothing, and it treated website claims, guides, calculators and bacteriostatic water sold alongside as evidence the products were meant for people. Counterfeit Ozempic in the legitimate supply chain The FDA warned three times about counterfeit Ozempic 1 mg that reached the normal US supply: lots NAR0074 (December 2023), PAR0362 (April 2025) and PAR1229 (December 2025). In the first batch the needles were counterfeit too, so sterility could not be confirmed. Salt forms instead of the active ingredient The FDA states that “semaglutide sodium” and “semaglutide acetate” are different active ingredients from semaglutide and that it is not aware of any lawful basis for using them. It also warns about products falsely labelled “for research” or “not for human consumption” sold straight to consumers. What was actually in products bought online In a study published in JAMA Network Open, semaglutide was test-purchased from six no-prescription vendors. Three orders never arrived. In the three that did, purity was 7 to 14 percent against an advertised 99, and content was 29 to 39 percent above the label. An independent analysis of melanotan II found 4.3 to 8.8 mg of peptide in vials labelled 10 mg. How to check this yourself The FDA runs an open database of products subject to recalls and warnings. You type a name and see the date, the firm, what the violation was and what action was taken. The agency itself notes the database covers only a fraction of the products on the market, so absence from it does not mean something is safe. “For research purposes only” A formula meant to shift responsibility onto the buyer. It is not a legal category that protects a seller: the FDA judged intended use by what the firm writes and what it sells alongside. A certificate that certifies nothing A scanned document with no laboratory name, date, batch number or method. The same file gets reused across sellers and batches. Before-and-after photos Lighting, time of day, hydration and muscle tension change appearance more than most substances do. Such photos prove nothing. A list of twenty effects The longer the list of promises, the weaker the evidence. It usually comes from cell or animal studies, at doses and routes that do not translate to people. A study that is not about the product A seller links a real paper, but it covers a different substance, a different form or only cells. It is worth opening the link and reading who was studied. Urgency and limits Countdown timers, “last units”, a discount only today. A sales device, not information about quality. Faceless reviews Reviews on a seller’s site are moderated by that seller. There is no way to know who wrote them or whether anyone received the same product. Vocabulary that dodges the law “Not for human consumption”, “reference material”, “reagent”. The wording changes the description, not what is inside or who it is sold to. Myth Research peptides bought online are the same as pharmacy medicines. “Research only” products do not have to meet the sterility, purity and dose-accuracy standards that apply to medicines. Vial contents may differ from the label, and batches are usually not independently checked. Myth If it is a natural peptide, it is safe. Insulin, glucagon and vasopressin are natural too, and the wrong dose can kill. Safety depends on dose, purity, route and human studies, not on where the molecule comes from. Myth BPC-157 is well studied in humans. A 2025 review found only 3 small human studies, under 30 people in total, without control groups. Almost all data come from animal studies. Myth In 2026 the FDA approved BPC-157 and TB-500. In July 2026 an FDA advisory committee only recommended adding them to the list of compounding ingredients (8 to 6). That is a non-binding recommendation, not drug approval, and it does not cover products from online shops. Myth Two GLP-1 drugs at once means faster weight loss. They act on the same receptor, so mainly side effects add up: nausea, vomiting, dehydration. The maker of tirzepatide states there are no data on combining it with other GLP-1 agonists. Myth After stopping an obesity drug the weight stays off. In withdrawal trials (STEP 4 for semaglutide, SURMOUNT-4 for tirzepatide) a large part of the lost weight returned within a year. These drugs work while they are taken. Partly true A peptide pill works just like an injection. Most peptides are digested in the stomach and gut. Exceptions such as oral semaglutide use a special absorption enhancer, need much higher doses and must be taken on an empty stomach. Partly true Collagen powder rebuilds your skin. A 2023 meta-analysis of 26 trials found a modest improvement in skin elasticity and hydration. Trials were small, some results subjective, and it does not replace sun protection. Partly true A certificate of analysis (CoA) guarantees quality. A CoA shows the result for one sample. If the seller issued it, without an independent lab and a batch number matching the package, it proves little. It does not replace sterility testing or drug-grade control. Myth Peptide cream works like Botox. Botulinum toxin is injected and blocks nerves in the muscle. Peptides in creams barely cross the epidermis, and evidence comes mostly from lab work and small manufacturer studies. Worth checking GLP-1 drugs are approved only for diabetes. Not true the other way round: several (Wegovy, Zepbound, Saxenda, and since 2026 the Foundayo pill) are separately approved for obesity, and Wegovy also for cardiovascular risk reduction. They are still prescription drugs under medical supervision.

32 questions about peptides, hormones and anabolic drugs, answered from the research — and about what we will not answer. Are peptides proteins? Peptides and proteins are made of the same amino acids. Peptides are shorter, proteins longer and folded into a stable structure. The border is conventional, often around 50 amino acids. Do peptides in creams reach the deeper skin? It depends on the molecule and carrier. Large molecules cross the epidermis poorly, so makers modify peptides, for example by attaching a fatty acid. Much of the data comes from lab studies. Why are peptide drugs usually injected? Peptides are digested by gut acid and enzymes, trapped by mucus and cross the gut lining poorly. An exception is semaglutide tablets, approved in 2019, which work with an absorption enhancer. Are peptides bought online safe? “Research only” products are not controlled like drugs and human data on them are scarce. Details are in the blog article. Does collagen powder work? A 2023 meta-analysis points to a modest gain in skin elasticity and hydration in healthy adults, but trials were small and partly subjective. It does not replace treatment. Where can I buy peptides? Approved peptide drugs are available only by prescription, from a pharmacy, after a doctor's decision. Substances sold as “research only” are not medicines: they lack drug-grade quality control and are not approved for human use. This site lists no shops, links or prices for peptides. How are lyophilized peptides stored? General rule for lyophilized powders: cool, dry, tightly sealed, away from light and moisture. After reconstitution peptides are usually much less stable. For a medicine, the exact conditions are in its leaflet, not in general rules. What is the difference between purity and peptide content? Purity (e.g. by HPLC) tells what share of the peptide material is the target peptide rather than related peptides. Peptide content tells what share of the vial mass is peptide at all, the rest being salts, water and excipients. High purity therefore does not mean the labelled mass is all active substance. How do I read a certificate of analysis (CoA)? Check: name and batch number matching the package, date, method (HPLC for purity, mass spectrometry for identity), result and who tested. A certificate issued by the seller without an independent lab proves little, and a CoA neither makes a substance a medicine nor replaces quality control. Can I ask about a dose or how to use something? We do not answer those. For most substances in the catalog no safe human dose has been established, and the numbers circulating on forums and from sellers are guesswork. We give doses only for approved drugs, copied from current labels, in the Dosing tab. Which seller is trustworthy? We do not recommend sellers and we do not run rankings. “Research” products are not medicines and nobody checks their contents or sterility. The Alerts tab collects FDA documents and studies showing what such products contain. What does “for research purposes only” mean? To the FDA, nothing. In warning letters the agency stated plainly that such a label does not change a product’s status when everything around it shows it is meant for people: effect claims, guides, calculators or bacteriostatic water sold alongside. I have a worrying symptom after a peptide. What should I do? We cannot assess symptoms over a message and we do not replace a doctor. For severe or sudden symptoms call emergency services. Tell the doctor exactly what was taken and when, even if it came from the internet. You can also describe the symptom in our form; reports are not published. Does a certificate of analysis (COA) mean a product is safe? No. A COA describes one sample, not a whole batch, and says nothing about sterility or whether the tested sample came from what you receive. Such documents also get copied between sellers. Independent analyses of products bought online found purity in the low tens of percent against an advertised 99. Is peptide X banned in sport? Check the anti-doping checker in the Catalog tab. It shows the WADA class and whether the ban applies at all times. Watch for the S0 clause: it covers substances with no approval for human treatment, even when they are not named. Why don’t you say something works when people say it helped them? Because individual reports cannot separate a substance’s effect from time, rehabilitation, a change in training or placebo. That is why each entry shows how many human trials are actually registered, with sources so anyone can check. Can I advertise my product here? No. We do not work with peptide sellers and we do not publish ads or shop links. The catalog is free and funded by our optional PDF guides, with no commission from anyone. What is the difference between anabolic steroids and corticosteroids? Anabolic steroids copy testosterone and build muscle and bone. Corticosteroids, such as prednisone, copy cortisol and calm inflammation and the immune system. They are different drugs with different risks, and they are often mixed up. Are peptides steroids? No. Peptides are short chains of amino acids, while steroids are fat-derived hormones with a four-ring core. Insulin and semaglutide are peptide drugs and neither is a steroid. Are anabolic steroids legal in the UK and the US? They are controlled drugs: Class C in the UK and Schedule III in the US. A doctor can prescribe some of them, such as testosterone, for a diagnosed condition, but supplying them without authority is an offence in both countries. Is it a crime to have steroids for personal use in the UK? In the UK, having anabolic steroids for your own use is not an offence in itself, but producing, supplying or offering to supply them is, and the rules on importing are strict. In the US, having them without a prescription is a federal offence. Laws change, so check current official guidance. What does “anabolic-androgenic” mean? Anabolic means building tissue, such as muscle and bone. Androgenic means producing male traits, such as a deeper voice and body hair. Every anabolic steroid has both effects, in different proportions. Is medical testosterone the same as steroid misuse? No. Testosterone replacement is a prescribed treatment for a proven deficiency, aimed at bringing levels back to the normal range and monitored with blood tests. Misuse means taking androgens without a medical reason, often in amounts far above what a doctor would prescribe. What are SARMs, and are they steroids? SARMs, or selective androgen receptor modulators, are lab compounds meant to act on muscle and bone more selectively than steroids. They are not steroids, none is approved as a medicine, and regulators have warned about products sold under these names. Can steroids cause permanent damage? Some effects can last. A deeper voice and some body-hair changes in women often do not reverse, heart changes can persist, and recovery of natural testosterone and fertility can be slow or incomplete. Teenagers who are still growing can end up shorter because the growth plates close early. Do steroids affect fertility? Yes. Anabolic steroids tell the brain to stop the signals that make the testes work, so sperm production can fall sharply. In many men it recovers within months after stopping, but in some it takes much longer or does not fully return. Why are steroids prohibited in sport? They give an unfair advantage and carry health risks, so WADA bans anabolic agents at all times, in and out of competition. A first intentional violation can bring a ban of up to four years. An athlete who needs a banned medicine for a real illness can apply for a therapeutic use exemption beforehand. Why do some prescription drugs for breast cancer and fertility appear in steroid discussions? Terms that come up on every page, explained once so the rest of the site reads easily. "Research use only" A label on products sold as laboratory reagents. It means the product is not a medicine and has not passed the quality and sterility checks required for medicines. Adverse effect A harmful or unwanted effect of a medicine or substance. Trials record all such events, including ones not proven to be caused by the substance. Agonist A substance that activates a receptor the way a natural signal does. Amino acid A building block of peptides and proteins. The body uses 20 standard ones. Analog A substance similar to a natural molecule, chemically modified, often to last longer. Antagonist A substance that blocks a receptor without activating it. Approved drug A substance authorised by a regulator (e.g. FDA, EMA) for a stated use. Bioavailability The share of a substance that reaches the blood in active form. Most peptides have very low bioavailability when swallowed, because enzymes digest them. Certificate of analysis (COA) A document with test results for a product batch. Its value depends on who tested it and how; a certificate issued by the seller itself proves little. Clinical trial phase Stages of testing a medicine in people. Phase 1: safety in a small group. Phase 2: whether it works and at what amount. Phase 3: large comparative trials before approval. Phase 4: monitoring after it reaches the market. Compounded drug A medicine prepared by a pharmacy for a specific patient rather than made in a factory. In the US, compounded drugs are not reviewed by the FDA like standard medicines. Concentration Mass of substance divided by solution volume, e.g. mg/ml. Control group Study participants who do not get the tested substance (they get placebo or standard care). Without one, it is impossible to tell whether an improvement came from the substance. DEXA A low-dose X-ray scan of body composition. It measures fat, lean mass and bone; shifts in water and glycogen can exaggerate short-term lean-mass loss. Double-blind A study in which neither participants nor researchers know who gets the medicine and who gets placebo. This reduces the influence of expectations on the results. Dual and triple agonist A molecule that activates two (for example GLP-1 and GIP) or three (GLP-1, GIP and glucagon) different receptors at once. More receptors can mean a stronger effect, but also more unknowns about safety. Endotoxin A fragment of the bacterial cell wall that can cause fever and inflammation even after the bacteria are dead. Medicines are tested for endotoxins; "research" products often are not. GIP The second incretin hormone from the gut (glucose-dependent insulinotropic polypeptide). It boosts insulin release after meals. Tirzepatide acts on both GIP and GLP-1 receptors. GLP-1 A gut hormone (glucagon-like peptide-1) released after meals. It raises glucose-dependent insulin release, slows stomach emptying and reduces appetite. Natural GLP-1 breaks down within minutes, so medicines use longer-lasting analogues. Glucagon A pancreatic hormone that raises blood glucose and increases energy use by the liver. Retatrutide and survodutide also act on the glucagon receptor, which is meant to raise energy expenditure. Growth hormone secretagogue A substance that prompts the pituitary gland to release growth hormone. This group includes GHRH analogues and ghrelin mimetics. Half-life Time for the blood concentration of a substance to fall by half. IGF-1 Insulin-like growth factor 1, made mainly by the liver in response to growth hormone. It carries out many of growth hormone's effects; its level is used to assess the growth hormone axis. Incretins Gut hormones that increase insulin release after a meal. The main ones are GLP-1 and GIP. Incretin medicines mimic their action. Indication The disease or condition a medicine is approved for. Off-label use has not been assessed by the regulator for that purpose. Lean mass Everything in the body except fat: muscle, organs, bone and water. With fast weight loss, part of the weight lost is lean mass. Lyophilizate A substance freeze-dried under vacuum and supplied as a powder in a vial. Melanocortins A group of hormones and receptors (MC1R–MC5R) that affect skin pigmentation, appetite and sexual function, among others. Afamelanotide and bremelanotide act on them. Meta-analysis An analysis that combines the results of many studies on the same question. It gives a stronger conclusion than one study, provided the studies were of good quality. Off-label Using an approved medicine for a different condition, amount or patient group than its label states. Doctors may prescribe this way, but the evidence is often weaker. Overdose Taking more than is safe. Symptoms need urgent help. Peptide A short chain of amino acids joined by peptide bonds. Usually up to about 50 residues; longer chains are proteins. Placebo An inactive substance given to a control group to separate the real effect of a medicine from expectation and chance. Studies without placebo or a control group give weak evidence. Preclinical study Research in cells or animals before a substance is tested in people. Most results at this stage are not confirmed later in humans. Prescribing information (label) The official document for a medicine approved by a regulator: uses, dosing, contraindications and side effects. In the US it is the label on DailyMed; in the EU and UK it is the SmPC. Purity (HPLC) The percentage of a sample made up of one compound, measured by chromatography. High purity does not say whether it is the right compound; that needs an identity test such as mass spectrometry. RCT Randomised controlled trial with a control group (placebo). Usually the strongest evidence of effect. Receptor A protein on or inside a cell that a specific molecule fits like a key in a lock. Binding triggers a specific response in the cell. Reconstitution Dissolving the powder in a solvent before use. It changes concentration, not the amount of substance. Regulators (FDA, EMA, MHRA) Agencies that approve medicines: the FDA in the US, the EMA in the European Union and the MHRA in the UK. Approval in one country does not mean approval in another. Sterility The absence of living microorganisms in a product. It is required for medicines given by routes that bypass the gut; without it there is a risk of infection. Systematic review A structured collection of all studies on a topic, gathered by set rules. It shows how much is known and how strong the evidence is. Tachyphylaxis A rapid loss of effect when the same substance is given repeatedly. It affects, for example, some growth-hormone-releasing peptides. WADA World Anti-Doping Agency. Publishes the list of substances banned in sport. WADA S0 list The WADA Prohibited List category for substances not approved for human use. It covers many peptides sold "for research".

t: Steroids and the law in the UK and the US
x: Anabolic steroids are controlled drugs in both countries, but the rules differ in how they treat having them and supplying them. This is a plain-language summary, not legal advice, and laws change. United Kingdom Anabolic steroids are Class C drugs under the Misuse of Drugs Act 1971. Producing or supplying them, or offering to, is a criminal offence that can carry a prison sentence. Having them for your own use is not an offence in itself, but that does not make them safe or legal to sell, share or bring in for others, and the rules on importing are strict. Check the current government guidance. United States Anabolic steroids are Schedule III controlled substances under federal law, after the Anabolic Steroid Control Acts of 1990 and 2004. Having them without a valid prescription is a federal offence, and distributing them carries heavier penalties. The 2004 law added steroid precursors, such as androstenedione, to the list after they had been sold as supplements. What a doctor can prescribe Testosterone is a legal medicine when a doctor prescribes it for a diagnosed condition such as hypogonadism. The same is true of corticosteroids and the hormone-modulating drugs that appear in this section. SARMs are different: they are not approved medicines, and selling them for human use can break medicines law even though they are not controlled drugs. Sport Rules in sport are separate from the law. WADA bans anabolic agents and many related drugs at all times, and a first intentional violation can bring a ban of up to four years. Athletes who need a banned medicine for a real illness can apply for a therapeutic use exemption before they use it. This section is information, not advice. t: What steroids do to the body, system by system
x: The harm from anabolic steroids is not one problem but a set of them, spread across the heart, liver, hormones, skin and mind. This page walks through each system and what the evidence shows, with the caveat that most of it comes from people taking far more than a doctor would prescribe. Heart and blood vessels Long-term heavy use is linked to a thickened heart muscle, weaker pumping, higher blood pressure and a fall in protective HDL cholesterol with a rise in LDL. These changes raise the risk of heart attack and sudden cardiac death, and cases have been reported in young and otherwise healthy athletes. Thicker blood, caused by a higher red blood cell count, adds to the risk of clots. Liver The oral steroids that are chemically altered to survive the liver carry the main risk. They can cause cholestasis, where bile cannot drain, benign and malignant liver tumours and peliosis hepatis, in which blood-filled cysts form in the liver. Injectable forms and gels are less toxic to the liver, but they have other risks. Hormones and fertility Taking an anabolic steroid tells the brain to stop sending the signals that make the testes work. Natural testosterone falls, the testes shrink and sperm production can drop sharply. After stopping, recovery can take months, and in some people it is incomplete, leaving low testosterone that needs medical treatment. Some steroids also convert to oestrogen, which can cause breast tissue growth in men. Mind and mood Some people report irritability, aggression and mood swings during use, and low mood or depression when levels fall. A minority develop a dependence, with difficulty stopping despite harm. Not everyone is affected the same way, and the research is mixed on how common the severe effects are. Skin, hair and tendons Acne, oily skin and stretch marks are common. In people with a family tendency, hair loss on the scalp can start or speed up. Muscle can grow faster than tendons can adapt, and steroid use has been linked to a higher risk of tendon rupture. Women and teenagers In women, androgens can deepen the voice, thicken body and facial hair, disturb periods and enlarge the clitoris, and some of these changes do not reverse when the drug is stopped. In teenagers who are still growing, steroids can close the growth plates early, which limits adult height. Risks that do not come from the drug itself Products from the illegal market can be counterfeit, mislabelled or contaminated. Injecting also brings the risk of infection, abscesses and nerve damage, and sharing needles can spread blood-borne viruses such as HIV and hepatitis. This is one reason doctors ask people to talk openly about what they are taking, so that blood tests and care can be matched to it. This section is information, not advice. t: Steroids vs peptides: what is the difference?
x: “Are peptides steroids?” is one of the most common questions we get, and the answer is no. They are different kinds of molecule, they act through different routes, and they are regulated differently. They get mixed up because they share markets, forums and banned lists. Being injected does not make something a steroid. Insulin and semaglutide are injected peptides, and neither is a steroid. What matters is the molecule and what it does inside the body. Aspect Steroids Peptides Chemistry A fat-derived molecule with a four-ring core, made from cholesterol. A short chain of amino acids, like a small protein. How it acts Passes into cells and switches genes on through hormone receptors inside them. Binds a receptor on the cell surface and sends a signal inward. Taken by mouth? Often yes, because many steroids survive digestion, sometimes at a cost to the liver. Usually no, because digestion breaks peptides down, so most are injected. Best-known medical uses Testosterone replacement, delayed puberty, some anaemias and muscle loss in illness. Diabetes, obesity, osteoporosis, fertility treatment and growth disorders. Regulation Anabolic steroids are controlled drugs (Class C in the UK, Schedule III in the US). Approved peptide drugs are prescription medicines. Unapproved “research” peptides sit in a grey zone and are not licensed for human use. Evidence for the “gym” uses Large, well documented effect on muscle, and a long record of harm at high doses. Mostly thin or animal-only for the unapproved ones, so both benefit and harm are largely unknown. Anti-doping Anabolic agents, category S1, prohibited at all times. Peptide hormones and growth factors, category S2, and some are in other categories. Prohibited at all times. Steroids: Advantages Well understood: decades of data on what they do and what they cost. Some are proven medicines, such as testosterone replacement for a diagnosed deficiency. Many can be taken by mouth. Steroids: Disadvantages Wide range of hormonal, heart, liver and mental-health risks at high or repeated use. Switch off the body’s own hormone production, and recovery can be slow or incomplete. Controlled drugs, with legal consequences for supply and, in some countries, possession. Peptides: Advantages Approved peptide drugs have large trials behind them, for diabetes, obesity and more. They usually act on one specific signal, so effects are easier to explain. Most are not controlled drugs, and approved ones are available through a doctor. Peptides: Disadvantages Most “research” peptides have no human safety data at all. Almost all need injection, and products of unknown purity are a risk of their own. Being unregulated is not the same as being safe. Common mix-ups Do peptides have fewer risks than steroids? Not by default. For steroids the risks are well mapped. For unapproved peptides they are mostly unmapped, and “we do not know” is not the same as “safe”. Is semaglutide a steroid? No. It is a peptide drug that copies the gut hormone GLP-1. It has nothing to do with testosterone or muscle building. Are SARMs steroids? No, they are a separate class of small molecules designed to hit androgen receptors more selectively. They are not approved as medicines, and regulators warn about them. Are prednisone and dexamethasone the same as anabolic steroids? No. They are corticosteroids that calm inflammation and do not build muscle. Long use brings its own risks, such as weaker bones and higher blood sugar. This section is information, not advice. x: A reference to anabolic steroids and the drugs sold alongside them: what each one is, what it was made for, how it is regulated and what the evidence says about the risks. Most of these drugs are controlled or prescription-only, and the safe way to any hormone treatment is a doctor. Two families, one name “Steroid” means a molecule with a four-ring core. Anabolic steroids copy testosterone and build muscle; corticosteroids copy cortisol and calm inflammation. They are different drugs with different risks. Not the same as peptides Peptides are short chains of amino acids. Steroids are fat-derived hormones. Some people lump them together because they appear in the same markets and the same banned lists. Why the risks are real High, repeated use of anabolic steroids is linked to heart, liver, hormonal and mental-health problems. Medical doses given for a diagnosis are a different situation from doses taken for looks or sport. Explainer What steroids do to the body, system by system The harm from anabolic steroids is not one problem but a set of them, spread across the heart, liver, hormones, skin and mind. Explainer Steroids and the law in the UK and the US Anabolic steroids are controlled drugs in both countries, but the rules differ in how they treat having them and supplying them. Testosterone and its relatives given by injection. A few are real medicines (testosterone replacement), others are veterinary products or old drugs that were withdrawn. Several forms Testosterone Testosterone is the body’s main androgen, made mostly in the testes in men and in small amounts in the ovaries and adrenal glands in women. Injectable Testosterone cypionate Testosterone cypionate is testosterone joined to a fatty acid chain, called an ester, which makes it release slowly from the injection site. Injectable Testosterone enanthate Testosterone enanthate is another long-acting ester of testosterone and behaves very much like cypionate. Several forms Testosterone undecanoate Testosterone undecanoate is an ester with an unusually long action. Injectable Sustanon Sustanon is a brand-name blend of four different testosterone esters, from short to long acting, in one oil injection. Injectable Nandrolone decanoate Nandrolone decanoate is a long-acting anabolic steroid made from a testosterone-like molecule with one methyl group removed. Injectable Trenbolone Trenbolone is a very potent anabolic steroid made for cattle, where it is used as a growth implant. Injectable Boldenone Boldenone is an anabolic steroid related to testosterone, developed for veterinary use, mainly in horses. Injectable Drostanolone Drostanolone is a derivative of dihydrotestosterone, the potent androgen made from testosterone. Injectable Methenolone enanthate Methenolone enanthate is a long-acting injectable form of a mild anabolic steroid derived from dihydrotestosterone. Injectable Testosterone propionate Testosterone propionate is a short-acting ester of testosterone. Injectable Nandrolone phenylpropionate Nandrolone phenylpropionate is a short-acting ester of the anabolic steroid nandrolone. Injectable Trestolone Trestolone, also called MENT, is a very potent synthetic androgen made from nandrolone. Tablets and capsules. Most are chemically altered so they survive the liver, and that alteration is also why many of them are hard on it. Oral Oxandrolone Oxandrolone is an oral anabolic steroid with relatively weak androgenic effects. Oral Methandienone Methandienone is one of the first anabolic steroids made for people, developed in the 1950s. Several forms Stanozolol Stanozolol is a synthetic steroid derived from dihydrotestosterone, sold in tablet and injectable forms. Oral Oxymetholone Oxymetholone is a strong oral anabolic steroid that is still a licensed medicine in the US for certain anaemias. Oral Methyltestosterone Methyltestosterone is testosterone with one extra methyl group so that it can be swallowed. Oral Chlorodehydromethyltestosterone This is a synthetic oral steroid developed in East Germany in the 1960s and sold as Oral-Turinabol. Oral Mesterolone Mesterolone is a mild oral androgen derived from dihydrotestosterone. Oral Danazol Danazol is a synthetic steroid with weak androgen activity. Oral Methasterone Methasterone is a strong oral steroid derived from dihydrotestosterone. Topical Clostebol Clostebol is an anabolic steroid made by adding a chlorine atom to testosterone. Gels, precursors the body converts into hormones, and one menopause drug with anabolic activity. Different routes, same hormone system. Topical Testosterone gel Testosterone gel is rubbed onto the skin, usually on the shoulders, arms or abdomen, and absorbed into the blood over the day. Oral DHEA DHEA is a hormone made by the adrenal glands that the body turns into testosterone and oestrogen. Oral Androstenedione Androstenedione is a hormone made in the adrenal glands and gonads that is one step away from testosterone and oestrogen. Oral Tibolone Tibolone is a synthetic steroid used for menopause symptoms. Topical Dihydrotestosterone Dihydrotestosterone, or DHT, is a hormone the body makes from testosterone. Selective androgen receptor modulators were designed to act on muscle and bone with fewer hormonal side effects than steroids. None has been approved, and regulators keep warning about products sold under these names. Oral Ostarine Ostarine, also called enobosarm, is the best-known SARM. Oral Ligandrol Ligandrol, or LGD-4033, is an experimental SARM that was tested in early human trials and never approved. Oral RAD140 RAD140, also called testolone, is an experimental SARM that has only been studied in animals and lab work. Oral Andarine Andarine, also called S-4, is an early experimental SARM that was never developed into a medicine. Oral YK-11 YK-11 is a lab compound built on a steroid backbone that acts on the androgen receptor. Growth hormone, stimulants, fat burners and lab compounds that show up in the same circles. They are not steroids, and some of them are far more dangerous than the steroids themselves. Oral Cardarine Cardarine, or GW501516, is often grouped with SARMs but is a different kind of compound, a PPAR-delta agonist. Oral MK-677 MK-677, or ibutamoren, is an oral drug that raises growth hormone and IGF-1 by acting on the ghrelin receptor. Oral SR9009 SR9009 is a lab compound that acts on Rev-Erb, a protein that helps run the body clock and energy use. Injectable Somatropin Somatropin is lab-made human growth hormone, a protein of 191 amino acids. Oral Clenbuterol Clenbuterol is a stimulant that opens the airways. Oral DNP DNP, or 2,4-dinitrophenol, is an industrial chemical used in dyes and explosives. Oral Tadalafil Tadalafil is a PDE5 inhibitor taken by mouth. Oral Sildenafil Sildenafil is the first PDE5 inhibitor, launched as Viagra in 1998. Oral Dapoxetine Dapoxetine is a short-acting antidepressant-type drug (an SSRI) made for premature ejaculation. Oral Yohimbine Yohimbine is an alkaloid from the bark of an African tree. Oral Liothyronine Liothyronine is the active form of thyroid hormone, known as T3. Oral Phentermine Phentermine is a stimulant related to amphetamine that reduces appetite. Oral DMAA DMAA, or 1,3-dimethylamylamine, is a strong stimulant that was sold in pre-workout and “fat burner” supplements. Several forms Salbutamol Salbutamol, called albuterol in the US, is the common reliever inhaler for asthma. Oral Meldonium Meldonium is a drug made in Latvia, sold in Eastern Europe as Mildronate. Oral Modafinil Modafinil is a prescription drug that promotes wakefulness. Oral Piracetam Piracetam is the first of a family of compounds called racetams, and the drug that gave the word “nootropic” to the world. t: Amino acid, peptide, protein: what is the difference
x: Amino acids are the building blocks. Humans use 20 standard amino acids, each with an amino and a carboxyl group. When the carboxyl group of one joins the amino group of the next, a peptide bond forms and a molecule of water is released. Two amino acids make a dipeptide, three a tripeptide, and chains up to about 20 are called oligopeptides. Longer ones are polypeptides. The line between a long peptide and a protein is conventional. Often about 50 amino acids is used, or whether the chain folds into a stable structure on its own. Insulin shows how blurry the line is: it has 51 amino acids in two chains and is called both a peptide hormone and a small protein. t: Collagen powder: what the studies show
x: Hydrolyzed collagen is collagen broken by enzymes into short peptides. In the gut it is digested further into amino acids and di- and tripeptides, and some short fragments have been detected in blood after eating. A 2023 meta-analysis by Pu and colleagues covered 26 randomized trials and 1,721 healthy adults taking collagen for 2 to 12 weeks. It found better skin elasticity and hydration than placebo, with larger effects after more than 8 weeks. There are limits: trials were small, some elasticity measures were self-reported, and most used marine collagen. Collagen will not replace sun protection or treatment of skin disease. t: GLP-1 weight-loss medicines: a guide to semaglutide, tirzepatide and retatrutide
x: Key takeaways: semaglutide and tirzepatide are approved medicines; retatrutide is still in trials and approved nowhere. In the main trials, average weight loss was about 15% with semaglutide (68 weeks), about 21% with tirzepatide (72 weeks) and about 24% with retatrutide (48 weeks, phase 2). Side effects are mostly digestive. Much of the weight tends to come back after stopping. Products sold online as "research" versions are not the trial medicines. How they work. GLP-1 is a gut hormone released after meals. It increases insulin release when glucose is high, slows stomach emptying and reduces appetite through the brain. Natural GLP-1 lasts only minutes, so the medicines are modified versions that last about a week. Liraglutide (daily) and semaglutide (weekly) act on the GLP-1 receptor only. Tirzepatide adds a second receptor, GIP. Retatrutide adds a third, the glucagon receptor, which is meant to increase energy use. What the trials showed. In STEP 1 (NEJM 2021), adults with obesity on semaglutide lost on average 14.9% of body weight over 68 weeks, compared with 2.4% on placebo. In SURMOUNT-1 (NEJM 2022), tirzepatide at the highest level tested led to an average loss of 20.9% over 72 weeks, versus 3.1% on placebo. In a phase 2 trial of retatrutide (NEJM 2023), the highest level tested led to an average loss of 24.2% over 48 weeks. These are averages: some people lost much more, some much less. Approval status. Semaglutide is approved for weight management (Wegovy) and type 2 diabetes (Ozempic, Rybelsus). Tirzepatide is approved for weight management (Zepbound) and type 2 diabetes (Mounjaro). Liraglutide is approved as Saxenda and Victoza. Retatrutide, mazdutide and survodutide are investigational: phase 3 trials are running, and none of them is an approved medicine. Approval in one country does not mean approval in another. Side effects. The most common are nausea, diarrhoea, vomiting and constipation, usually early in treatment and while the amount is being increased. The labels also warn about gallbladder problems, pancreatitis, and dehydration from vomiting or diarrhoea. Resting heart rate rose by a few beats per minute in trials. Fast weight loss can include a meaningful share of muscle and other lean tissue, which is why guidance stresses protein and strength training. Stopping treatment. In a STEP 1 extension, people who stopped semaglutide regained about two-thirds of the lost weight within a year. Obesity behaves like a long-term condition, and these medicines work while they are taken. Online "research" versions. Products sold as "research use only" are not the medicines tested in trials. Nobody checks their identity, amount, purity or sterility, and the FDA has warned about counterfeit and unapproved versions. For retatrutide, which is approved nowhere, any product sold to the public is outside the trials. Every medicine in this guide has its own card in the PepSafe catalog with status, mechanism, evidence and sources, and the comparison pages set them side by side. Educational content, not medical advice: decisions about treatment belong with a doctor who knows your case. t: KLOW 80: what is in the vial and what we don't know
x: KLOW is a blend of four peptides in one vial: GHK-Cu , BPC-157 , TB-500 and KPV. The 80 is the total mass in milligrams. Sellers usually list 50 mg GHK-Cu and 10 mg each of BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV, but ratios vary between makers and nobody checks them independently. KLOW is essentially the GLOW blend (GHK-Cu, BPC-157, TB-500) plus KPV. Neither the blend nor any of its ingredients is an approved drug. No clinical trial of KLOW as a whole has been published. For the ingredients, evidence comes mostly from cell cultures and animal studies. For BPC-157, a 2025 review found only 3 small human studies, under 30 people in total, without control groups. Seller claims such as faster healing, regeneration and less inflammation are animal results carried over to people, not clinical data. Nobody has studied how the four substances act together: whether they add up, cancel out or cause new side effects. Concrete risks: a “research only” product does not have to meet drug standards for sterility and purity, so the vial may hold a different amount than labelled, impurities or endotoxins. Injecting a non-sterile solution risks infection. BPC-157 and TB-500 affect blood vessel growth, which could in theory matter with cancer. BPC-157 and TB-500 are on the WADA prohibited list. Legal status: in July 2026 an FDA advisory committee backed adding BPC-157, TB-500 and KPV to the list of substances pharmacies may compound. That is not drug approval, the FDA has not decided yet, and it does not cover ready-made blends from online shops. We give no KLOW dose, because none has been established in humans. Numbers online are guesswork. t: Peptides in cosmetics: studies versus marketing
x: Manufacturers usually split cosmetic peptides into signal peptides (meant to prompt skin cells to make collagen), carrier peptides such as copper-binding GHK-Cu , and neuromodulating ones such as acetyl hexapeptide-8, marketed as “Botox in a cream”. The catch is that much of the evidence comes from lab work, animal studies or small manufacturer-sponsored trials. A review describing GHK-Cu credits it with antioxidant and regenerative effects but rests mostly on in vitro and animal studies. Large molecules struggle to cross the epidermis, so formulation matters. It is reasonable to judge results after several weeks of regular use, not expect a clinic-level change, and patch-test on a small area of skin. t: “Research use only” peptides: why they are a bad idea
x: Peptides labelled “for laboratory research only”, such as BPC-157 , are sold online. Many are not approved as drugs. Such products need not meet drug manufacturing standards, so contents, purity, strength and sterility are hard to verify. Human data are very thin. A 2025 review cited by Prof. Stuart Phillips of McMaster University found only three human studies of BPC-157, with fewer than 30 participants in total and no control groups. Animal results often fail to carry over to people, there are no established doses, and side effects from longer use may take months or years to appear. What to do instead: peptide drugs such as insulin and GLP-1 analogues have approved uses and quality control but need a doctor's decision. For injuries, rehabilitation, sleep and enough dietary protein are proven. Athletes should note that many peptides and growth factors are on the WADA prohibited list. What it is Anastrozole is an aromatase inhibitor. It blocks the enzyme that turns testosterone into oestrogen and is used in breast cancer treatment. How it works By stopping oestrogen production in fat and other tissue, it lowers oestrogen levels sharply. That starves oestrogen-driven tumours. Medical use It is approved for hormone-receptor-positive breast cancer in women after menopause. Its use in men is off-label. Risks and side effects The label lists bone thinning and fractures, joint pain, hot flushes and higher cholesterol. Lowering oestrogen too far is harmful in men too, because oestrogen helps protect bones and affects mood and libido. What not to combine Do not combine with oestrogen-containing medicines or with tamoxifen, which counter its effect. Tell your doctor about every medicine you take, because strong hormone changes affect bones and cholesterol. Legal status Prescription-only medicines in the UK and the US. They are licensed for specific conditions, and using them for anything else is off-label and needs a doctor. Sport and anti-doping WADA prohibits hormone and metabolic modulators (category S4) or peptide hormones (category S2) at all times, depending on the substance. What it is Dexamethasone is a very potent, long-acting corticosteroid, given by mouth, injection or drops. It became widely known in 2020 for its role in severe COVID-19. What it is Liothyronine is the active form of thyroid hormone, known as T3. It is a prescription medicine for thyroid disease. Oral steroid known as “Turinabol” Oral anabolic steroids Oral Chemical structure (PubChem) This section is information, not advice. We give no doses, no routes to buy and no instructions for use. Most of these drugs are controlled or prescription-only, and the safe way to any hormone treatment is a doctor. What it is This is a synthetic oral steroid developed in East Germany in the 1960s and sold as Oral-Turinabol. It was at the centre of that country’s state doping programme. How it works It is a modified version of testosterone that acts on the androgen receptor and was designed to have weak androgenic effects. Like other oral steroids it is chemically altered to survive the liver. Medical use It is not an approved medicine today. Its modern profile comes mainly from doping investigations and long-term follow-up of former athletes. Risks and side effects Follow-up of athletes from the East German programme documented serious long-term harm, including liver problems and, in women, masculinising changes and fertility problems. Traces remain detectable for months, which is why retesting of old samples has caught athletes years later. What not to combine Do not combine with alcohol or with other drugs that strain the liver, including other oral steroids. Oral androgens of this kind can strengthen the effect of the blood thinner warfarin and raise the risk of bleeding, and they can change blood sugar control in people with diabetes. Legal status Not approved as a medicine anywhere today. It is a controlled anabolic steroid in the UK (Class C) and the US (Schedule III). Sport and anti-doping WADA prohibits anabolic agents (category S1) at all times, in and out of competition. t: The July 2026 FDA committee vote: what it really means for BPC-157 and others
x: On 22–23 July 2026 the FDA Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) reviewed seven peptides. It backed six: BPC-157 , TB-500 and KPV (each 8 to 6 with one abstention), plus MOTS-c , Semax and Epitalon . It rejected DSIP (emideltide) 6 to 7. What it means: the committee recommends adding these substances to the 503A list of bulk ingredients US pharmacies may compound on an individual prescription. The recommendation is non-binding. The FDA still has to run its own process, estimated at several months to over a year. What it does not mean: it is not drug approval. There are no phase 3 trials, established doses or indications. FDA staff raised safety and evidence concerns, and the votes were close. It applies only to US prescription compounding, not to “research” products from online shops or blends such as GLOW or KLOW . In Poland and the EU these substances are still not authorised as medicines. We will update the PepSafe catalog when the FDA makes a final decision. In depth Glucagon is a 29-amino-acid pancreatic hormone that does the opposite of insulin: when blood sugar falls, it tells the liver to release stored glucose. After stopping, most of the lost weight usually returns. The FDA has warned about counterfeit Ozempic and about 'semaglutide' in other salt forms sold outside pharmacies. Vancocin Approved drug Glycopeptide What it is A peptide antibiotic known since 1958. How it works Blocks cell wall building in Gram-positive bacteria. Use Gram-positive infections, including MRSA. What the research shows Approved drug. In depth Vancomycin is a glycopeptide antibiotic isolated in the 1950s from a soil bacterium from Borneo and approved in 1958. It blocks cell wall building in Gram-positive bacteria, including methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Given intravenously it treats serious Gram-positive infections, and by mouth, because it is then not absorbed, Clostridioides difficile infection. Blood levels need monitoring because it can damage the kidneys and hearing. Overuse has contributed to vancomycin-resistant enterococci (VRE). Vasostrict Approved drug Peptide hormone Anti-doping: S5 Vasopressin and its analogues Do not combine: duplicated vasopressin receptors Group What it is A nine-amino-acid antidiuretic hormone. How it works Binds V1 and V2 receptors (narrows vessels, retains water). Use Vasodilatory shock, given in hospital. What the research shows Approved drug. In depth Vasopressin is a 9-amino-acid hormone made in the hypothalamus and released from the pituitary. Through V1 receptors it narrows blood vessels, and through V2 receptors it makes the kidneys hold on to water, hence its other name: antidiuretic hormone. Vincent du Vigneaud's team worked out and synthesised its structure in the 1950s. As a medicine (in the US Vasostrict, formally approved in 2014) it is given by infusion in intensive care for shock when other drugs cannot hold blood pressure. Too much can starve fingers, gut or heart of blood. It has no use outside hospital. Aviptadil Unapproved Neuropeptide What it is A natural 28-amino-acid peptide. Aviptadil is its synthetic form with the same sequence, and it was studied in COVID-19, among others. How it works Widens blood vessels and modulates inflammation. Use Experimental. What the research shows Not approved. In depth VIP (vasoactive intestinal peptide) is a 28-amino-acid hormone discovered in 1970 by Sami Said and Viktor Mutt. It widens blood vessels, relaxes smooth muscle and drives water secretion in the gut; a VIP-secreting tumour (VIPoma) causes severe diarrhoea. Synthetic VIP, aviptadil, was studied for respiratory failure in COVID-19, among others, without convincing results, and was not approved there. In some countries aviptadil is part of an erectile dysfunction medicine injected into the penis. Injected, it can lower blood pressure sharply. Voxzogo Approved drug CNP analogue What it is FDA-approved in 2021. Increases long-bone growth in children with achondroplasia whose growth plates are still open. How it works Mimics natural CNP. Binds the NPR-B receptor and increases cGMP signaling in growth plate cartilage. Use Children with achondroplasia and open growth plates (accelerated approval). What the research shows Approved based on growth studies in children; long-term effects are still being studied. In depth Vosoritide from BioMarin is an analogue of C-type natriuretic peptide (CNP). It binds the NPR-B receptor in growth plate cartilage and counteracts the overactive FGFR3 receptor that slows long-bone growth in achondroplasia. The FDA approved it in 2021 (Voxzogo) for children with achondroplasia and open growth plates, and later widened the age range. In the phase 3 trial (Lancet 2020), children grew on average about 1.6 cm per year more than on placebo. It is injected under the skin daily; it can briefly lower blood pressure. In depth Ziconotide is a synthetic version of omega-conotoxin MVIIA, a 25-amino-acid peptide from the venom of the cone snail Conus magus. Zaltrap Not a peptide VEGF trap What it is This is a monoclonal antibody or fusion protein, not a peptide: a molecule hundreds of times larger than a peptide, grown in cells rather than made chemically. It appears here because peptide lists often include it. How it works Acts as an artificial receptor: it traps VEGF-A, VEGF-B and PlGF, cutting the tumour off from new blood vessels. Use Metastatic colorectal cancer, combined with FOLFIRI chemotherapy. What the research shows FDA approved in 2012 on the basis of the VELOUR trial. In depth Ziv-aflibercept is a fusion protein that acts as an artificial receptor: it traps the vessel growth factors VEGF-A, VEGF-B and PlGF and cuts the tumour off from new blood vessels. It is the same molecule as aflibercept used in eye disease (Eylea), but in a different form and dose. The FDA approved it in 2012 (Zaltrap) for metastatic colorectal cancer together with FOLFIRI chemotherapy, based on the VELOUR trial. Side effects include high blood pressure, bleeding, poor wound healing and, rarely, bowel perforation. Advantages Approved by the FDA in 2012 for metastatic colorectal cancer VELOUR trial supported approval Disadvantages Bleeding, high blood pressure and wound-healing problems Cancer treatment given only with chemotherapy What to watch for High blood pressure, bleeding, impaired wound healing, gastrointestinal perforation.
